lead: Knuckle and cotter joints connect two rods that pull apart. A knuckle joint uses a pin through an eye and a fork; the pin works in double shear and bearing. A cotter joint uses a tapered rectangular cotter through a socket and spigot; the cotter works in double shear and bearing. Each part is sized by its own failure mode, so rod, pin or cotter, eye, fork, socket and collar can have different critical sections. They appear in tie rods, turnbuckles, railway couplers and link mechanisms.
prereq: You need: tensile stress σ<sub>t</sub> = P/A, shear stress τ = P/A, bearing stress σ<sub>c</sub> = P/(projected area), and factor of safety from Unit 1.

sections.h3: Knuckle joint: four parts and one load path

blocks.text: A knuckle joint joins two rods on one axis and allows small angular movement. Rod 1 ends in an eye: a ring with a hole. Rod 2 ends in a fork: a U-shaped end with two eyes, called tines. The eye sits between the tines. A pin passes through all three holes. A head on one end and a split pin or collar on the other keeps the pin in place. Some syllabi call this pin a hinge pin.

When the rods pull with force P, the eye pulls the pin at its middle. The two fork tines pull the pin at two outer regions. The pin therefore has two shear planes, one between the eye and each tine. That is double shear. The pin also presses on the eye and tines over small contact areas; that is bearing. The eye is in tension across its net section beside the pin hole. The fork tines are in tension and bearing.
Tie rods of pandal frames, turnbuckles and link mechanisms use this joint.

sections.h3: Sizing the knuckle joint by failure mode

blocks.text: Size the rod first, then the pin, then check bearing and bending. Use P in newtons, diameters in millimetres, and stresses in N/mm², which is the same as MPa.

blocks.where: P is the tensile load in N; d is the rod diameter in mm; σ<sub>t</sub> is the rod tensile stress in N/mm².
d<sub>p</sub> is the pin diameter in mm; τ is the pin shear stress in N/mm²; the 2 is for two shear planes.
t<sub>e</sub> is eye thickness in mm; D<sub>e</sub> is eye outside diameter in mm; d<sub>p</sub> is pin diameter in mm.

blocks.text: Bearing (crushing) stress on the eye is σ<sub>c</sub> = P/(d<sub>p</sub>t<sub>e</sub>). Bearing on each fork tine is σ<sub>c</sub> = P/(2d<sub>p</sub>t<sub>f</sub>), where t<sub>f</sub> is one tine thickness in mm. Bending stress in the pin is σ<sub>b</sub> = M/Z. Treat the pin as a beam with P at the centre and P/2 at each tine. The lever arm is half the eye thickness plus half one tine thickness, so M = (P/2)(t<sub>e</sub>/2 + t<sub>f</sub>/2) = P(t<sub>e</sub> + t<sub>f</sub>)/4, with t<sub>e</sub> and t<sub>f</sub> in mm. Z = πd<sub>p</sub>³/32, where d<sub>p</sub> is pin diameter in mm.

Standard proportions are a starting point only. The stress checks decide the final sizes. If a syllabus gives proportions, use them to propose D<sub>e</sub>, t<sub>e</sub>, t<sub>f</sub> and then verify shear, bearing and bending.

A cotter joint also joins two rods in tension. Rod 1 ends in a socket: a hollow end with a slot. Rod 2 ends in a spigot: a smaller cylinder that fits into the socket. A flat rectangular cotter passes through slots in both parts. A collar on the spigot bears against the socket and stops the spigot from pulling out. The cotter is slightly tapered so it can be driven tight and later removed.

The load P pulls the socket left and the spigot right. The cotter bears on the socket slot and on the spigot slot. The cotter has two shear planes, one on each side of the spigot. The rod is in tension; the spigot is in tension across the cotter hole; the socket wall is in tension beside the slot; the collar is in bearing against the socket.

items: Cotter double shear: τ = P/(2bt) ≤ τ<sub>allow</sub>, where b is cotter width in mm and t is cotter thickness in mm.
Cotter bearing on spigot: σ<sub>c</sub> = P/(d<sub>s</sub>t) ≤ σ<sub>c,allow</sub>, where d<sub>s</sub> is spigot diameter in mm.
Rod tension: σ<sub>t</sub> = 4P/(πd²) ≤ σ<sub>t,allow</sub>, where d is rod diameter in mm.

Socket tearing: σ<sub>t</sub> = P/A<sub>net</sub> ≤ σ<sub>t,allow</sub>, where A<sub>net</sub> = (π/4)(D² − d<sub>s</sub>²) − (D − d<sub>s</sub>)t, with D the socket outside diameter in mm, d<sub>s</sub> the spigot diameter in mm and t the cotter thickness in mm.
Collar crushing: σ<sub>c</sub> = P/[(π/4)(D<sub>c</sub>² − d<sub>s</sub>²)] ≤ σ<sub>c,allow</sub>, where D<sub>c</sub> is collar outside diameter in mm.

blocks.text: Choose b and t from shear and bearing, then check the spigot, socket and collar. A cotter that passes shear can still crush the spigot, so both checks are needed.

figure.caption: The load sizes the knuckle rod and pin; bearing follows. A cotter joint uses the same load path but a flat cotter in double shear.

spec.title: Knuckle joint sizing
spec.aria: The tensile load first sizes the rod, then the pin in double shear, then the bearing areas of the eye and fork.

examples.question: A knuckle joint carries a rod tension P = 50 kN. The allowable tensile stress is 60 MPa and the allowable shear stress is 40 MPa. Find the rod diameter and the pin diameter for double shear. Round each up to the next even millimetre.
steps: P = 50 kN = 50 000 N; 60 MPa = 60 N/mm²; 40 MPa = 40 N/mm².
Pin double shear: shear area = 2 × πd<sub>p</sub>²/4 = πd<sub>p</sub>²/2. τ = P/(πd<sub>p</sub>²/2) = 2P/(πd<sub>p</sub>²).
Check bearing on the eye and fork after these sizes are fixed.
examples.answer: Rod diameter = 34 mm; pin diameter = 30 mm.
examples.check:
import math
P = 50_000
sigma_t = 60
tau = 40
d = math.sqrt(4 * P / (math.pi * sigma_t))
dp = math.sqrt(2 * P / (math.pi * tau))
d_choose = 2 * math.ceil(d / 2)
dp_choose = 2 * math.ceil(dp / 2)
print(f"{d:.1f}")
print(f"{dp:.1f}")
print(d_choose)
print(dp_choose)

traps: Using single shear for the knuckle pin. The pin has two shear planes, so the shear area is πd<sub>p</sub>²/2, not πd<sub>p</sub>²/4.
Taking the rod diameter as the pin diameter. The rod is sized by tension; the pin is sized by double shear, so the two sizes differ.
Skipping the bearing check after choosing a pin. A pin that passes in shear can still crush the eye or fork.
Using the cotter width b in the shear formula when the thickness t is meant, or forgetting the factor 2. The cotter has two shear planes, τ = P/(2bt).

quiz.q: Name the four main parts of a knuckle joint.
quiz.a: Rod with eye, rod with fork, pin, and pin retainer (head and split pin or collar).

quiz.q: Why is the knuckle pin in double shear?
quiz.a: The eye pulls the pin at the middle; the two fork tines support it on either side, so two cross-sections carry the load.

quiz.q: A cotter joint carries P = 30 kN. The cotter has width b = 20 mm and thickness t = 8 mm. Find the shear stress in the cotter.
A knuckle pin diameter is doubled while P stays the same. What happens to the shear stress?
quiz.a: The shear area becomes four times larger, so the shear stress becomes one quarter of its old value.

quiz.q: Write the bearing stress formula for the eye of a knuckle joint.
quiz.a: σ<sub>c</sub> = P/(d<sub>p</sub>t<sub>e</sub>), where d<sub>p</sub> is pin diameter and t<sub>e</sub> is eye thickness.

quiz.q: Why does a cotter joint use a flat cotter rather than a round pin?
quiz.a: A flat cotter gives a large rectangular bearing area and can be tapered to wedge tight and be removed; it is easy to make in a slot.

quiz.q: A knuckle joint carries P = 60 kN. Pin diameter is 25 mm. Find the shear stress in double shear.
In a cotter joint, why is the socket checked for tearing rather than only for crushing?
quiz.a: The cotter slot removes material from the socket, so the remaining wall carries tension P; the net section may tear before bearing fails.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production knuckle joints are sized with standard tables, then checked by finite element contact analysis because the pin-eye contact is not uniform. Fretting and corrosion at the pin hole often decide the life of railway couplers and suspension links. Cotter joints survive in older tie rods and turnbuckles because they are easy to assemble without threads. Search for knuckle joint fillet stress concentration, cotter joint fretting fatigue, and pin bearing contact pressure.
